questions.q: Why is accuracy a poor metric for anomaly detection?
options: Anomalies are rare, so predicting 'normal' always gives high accuracy
why: It can be computed; it just misleads.

questions.q: 5 true events, 8 alarms. 4 events are found, 6 alarms overlap a true event. What is the event precision?
questions.why: Precision = alarms that touch a true event / all alarms = 6 / 8 = 0.75.

questions.q: What is wrong with point adjustment?
options: One hit inside an event marks all its points as detected, which inflates scores
why: It is a scoring step, not a model.

questions.q: Scenario: a paper claims F1 = 0.9 using point adjustment. A random detector with 3% flagged points scores 0.8 with the same method. What do you conclude?
options: The paper's gain over random is small; the metric is weak
The paper is wrong about everything
why: Correct: compare with baselines under the same metric.
Not necessarily; the metric is the issue.
They are not good; the metric is lenient.

questions.q: Scenario: a fraud alert arrives 2 hours after the fraud. Which scoring idea captures that this is worth less?
options: NAB: earlier detection in the window earns more

questions.q: In NAB, what happens with a false alarm outside every anomaly window?
why: It is counted as a penalty.
